course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes popular attitudes toward expansion in the United States in the 1840s?
choices: Most Americans agreed that growth should stop at the borders set by the Louisiana Purchase
Enthusiasm for new land, supported by economic and security interests, was widespread
Congress opposed all expansion because defending new lands would cost too much money
Business leaders opposed expansion because they feared a loss of trade with Europe
questions.explanation: Many Americans supported expansion for economic opportunity and security, and the nation grew to the Pacific.
choiceExplanations: Settlers and leaders pushed the nation's borders to the Pacific.
Many Americans supported expansion for economic opportunity and security, and the nation grew to the Pacific.
Congress voted to annex Texas and to pay for the war with Mexico.
Business leaders wanted new land and trade with Asia.
questions.distinguisher: The Louisiana Purchase choice is close because earlier leaders expected gradual growth, but by the 1840s popular enthusiasm pressed the borders to the Pacific.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following questions did Americans continue to debate in the 1840s and 1850s?
choices: Whether to bring back property requirements for voting in the Northern states
Whether the nation should replace the Constitution with a new plan of government
Whether the president should be chosen by Congress and not by electors
What rights and citizenship women, immigrants, and African Americans should have
questions.explanation: Questions about the rights of women, immigrants, American Indians, and African Americans, enslaved and free, stayed at the center of public debate.
choiceExplanations: Most states had already dropped those requirements.
No major group sought to replace the Constitution.
Americans did not seriously debate that change.
Questions about the rights of women, immigrants, American Indians, and African Americans, enslaved and free, stayed at the center of public debate.
questions.distinguisher: The property requirements choice is close because voting rights were a major question in the early 1800s, but most states had dropped those rules for white men.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The sectional conflict of the 1850s is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: Territorial expansion that raised the question of whether slavery would spread to new lands
A dispute with Britain over the northern boundary of the Oregon country
A struggle between rural and urban voters for control of the Electoral College
A plan to end the tariff and to tax the land of Southern planters
questions.explanation: Each new territory raised the question of slavery, and the debate hardened the differences between the North and the South.
choiceExplanations: Each new territory raised the question of slavery, and the debate hardened the differences between the North and the South.
That dispute ended in 1846 and did not divide North from South.
The sections, not city and country, were the main divide.
No such plan was before the nation.
questions.distinguisher: The Oregon boundary choice is close because it was part of the era's expansion, but it was settled by treaty and did not involve slavery.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context.

questions.prompt: Which of the following helps to explain the rise in migration from Europe to the United States in the 1840s and 1850s?
choices: A federal program that paid for the voyage of European families to the American West
The closing of European ports to trade with the United States after the Mexican War
Famine, poverty, and political upheaval in Europe, especially in Ireland and Germany
A treaty that gave Irish families the right to settle in Canada before the United States
questions.explanation: Hardship at home pushed many Irish and German families to cross the Atlantic, and the United States offered work and land.
choiceExplanations: No such program existed.
European ports stayed open to American trade.
Hardship at home pushed many Irish and German families to cross the Atlantic, and the United States offered work and land.
No treaty directed Irish families to Canada.
questions.distinguisher: The federal program choice is close because land policy did attract settlers, but the government did not pay for the voyage of migrants.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The Civil War and Reconstruction changed the relationship between the states and the federal government by
choices: confirming that a state could leave the Union if a majority of its voters wished
increasing federal authority, including its power to protect the rights of citizens
ending the power of Congress to tax and to regulate trade among the states
giving state legislatures the power to cancel acts of Congress they thought unfair
questions.explanation: The Union victory and the new amendments gave the federal government more authority over the states.
choiceExplanations: The Union victory settled the issue of secession.
The Union victory and the new amendments gave the federal government more authority over the states.
Congress kept those powers.
The war ended arguments for nullification.
questions.distinguisher: The secession choice is close because the question of leaving the Union was the cause of the war, but the war settled it against secession.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a continuity from the 1840s through the 1870s?
choices: People held in the Southern states remained the legal property of their owners
The Whig Party remained one of the two major parties in every region
American Indians were treated as citizens with a right to vote in federal elections
Americans debated the rights of women, African Americans, and other groups
questions.explanation: Questions about who held rights and citizenship continued from before the war through Reconstruction.
choiceExplanations: The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery in 1865.
The Whigs collapsed in the 1850s.
American Indians were not generally citizens in this period.
Questions about who held rights and citizenship continued from before the war through Reconstruction.
questions.distinguisher: The legal property choice is close because slavery was the central issue before the war, but it ended in 1865 and so was a change, not a continuity.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following helped the Union to win the Civil War?
choices: Its greater manpower and industry and Lincoln's decision to emancipate enslaved people
Control of the cotton crop, which paid for the Union's war effort
Troops from Britain and France that were sent to fight for the North
A treaty with the Confederacy that divided the western territories
questions.explanation: The North's population and factories, strong leadership, and the decision to emancipate led to the Union's victory.
choiceExplanations: The North's population and factories, strong leadership, and the decision to emancipate led to the Union's victory.
The Confederacy grew nearly all of the cotton.
Neither European power sent troops to the Union.
No such treaty was made.
questions.distinguisher: The cotton choice is close because cotton was the South's best-known resource, but the Confederacy controlled it and could not turn it into a victory.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Debates in the 1860s and 1870s over citizenship for African Americans are best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: The Dred Scott decision, which had already confirmed that African Americans were citizens
A treaty with Britain that required the United States to extend the vote to Black men
The end of slavery through the Civil War and the Thirteenth Amendment
A decision by Southern states in 1865 to rejoin the Union without any conditions
questions.explanation: Once slavery had ended, the nation had to decide what rights the formerly enslaved would hold.
choiceExplanations: Dred Scott held that they were not citizens.
No treaty required it.
Once slavery had ended, the nation had to decide what rights the formerly enslaved would hold.
Congress set conditions for readmission.
questions.distinguisher: The Dred Scott choice is close because the case addressed citizenship, but it held the opposite and was overturned by the Fourteenth Amendment.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.
